modules.title: The Big Picture
modules.goal: Know what a software factory is and the shape of Gas City.

modules.title: Work: Beads
modules.goal: Understand the unit of work, how it is ordered, grouped and claimed.

modules.title: Workers: Agents and Sessions
modules.goal: Define agents, run sessions and see how agents coordinate.

modules.title: Methods: Formulas
modules.goal: Write a method once and let the orchestrator run it as a graph.

modules.goal: Make the factory start, supervise and observe its own work.

modules.goal: Package, share and assemble the whole factory.

days.title: Software Factory vs. Coding Agent
days.what: A software factory runs a written-down method across a fleet of coding agents, without you steering every step.
what_points: Runs without you in the loop
days.why: One coding agent is a faster pair of hands, but it works alone, needs you watching, and loses context when it crashes.
why_points: One session, one train of thought
days.how: You write the method once; an orchestrator splits the job into tracked work, runs independent pieces in parallel and retries failures.
how_points: Orchestrator splits the job into tracked units
Parallel where possible, wait where needed
Retry until the job is done

visual.caption: Faster hands vs. a system that produces finished work

days.analogy: A great chef cooks one meal fast. A restaurant kitchen has recipes, stations and tickets, so dinner is served even when one cook goes home.

jargon.plain: the program that hands out work, tracks it and keeps it moving
many coding agents working at the same time

days.takeaway: A coding agent gives you faster hands; a software factory gives you finished work without you in the loop.
days.artifact: Sketch two columns on paper: interactive session vs. software factory. The HOW slide is that sketch.
verify: docs/index.mdx describes Gas City as the platform for building software factories.
The FAQ promise: describe a feature once and come back to a finished branch.

days.title: Gas City: Zero Hardcoded Roles
days.what: Gas City is an open-source toolkit for building software factories: orchestration infrastructure for multi-agent coding.
what_points: A toolkit, not one fixed bot
days.why: Hardcoded roles lock you into someone else's team shape. Gas City makes every role configuration, so one engine runs many designs.
days.how: The engine only knows primitives; packs supply the roles. Swap the packs and you get a different factory, Gas Town included.
how_points: Gas Town is one pack on top
Your team shape is your pack

layers.label: Your factory
layers.sub: Gas Town · Ralph · your own design

visual.caption: Roles live in packs, not in the binary

days.analogy: Like a game engine: the engine handles physics and drawing; each game brings its own characters.

jargon.plain: a toolkit you build your own product with
a folder of config that defines agents, methods and schedules

days.takeaway: Gas City hardcodes zero roles, so you can build the factory your team actually needs.
days.artifact: Open the Gas Town role table in coming-from-gastown.md and pick two roles to mention: Mayor and Polecat.
verify: how-gas-city-works.md: the orchestrator hardcodes zero roles.
README and FAQ: Gas City is MIT-licensed.
coming-from-gastown.md: every Gas Town role maps to a configured agent.

days.title: The Six Primitives
days.what: Everything in Gas City is built from six primitives: Agent, Bead, Formula, Rig, Pack and Event.
days.why: Six words give you a map. Every feature you meet later is one of them, or a combination of them.
why_points: New features slot into the map
days.how: Packs declare agents and formulas; a formula operates over beads; agents execute beads in a rig; events fire so everyone can watch.
how_points: Agents execute beads in a rig
Events let humans and agents observe

visual.caption: The six primitives and how they relate

days.analogy: Who, what, how and where are the questions every news story answers. Add who set it up and how you hear about it.

jargon.plain: a basic building block that isn't made of smaller blocks

days.takeaway: Who, what, how, where, configure, observe: six primitives hold the whole system.
days.artifact: The primitives diagram. Practise pointing at each box in order: Pack, Formula, Bead, Agent, Rig, Event.
verify: The six-primitives table in how-gas-city-works.md: Agent WHO, Bead WHAT, Formula HOW, Rig WHERE, Pack CONFIGURES, Event OBSERVE.

days.title: The Machinery Underneath
days.what: Three pieces of plumbing run the primitives: the orchestrator, the bead store and the event bus.
days.why: If progress lived inside an agent's memory, one crash would erase it. In shared state, work survives a crash on either side.
days.how: The orchestrator starts and stops sessions, but reads their progress from the store and event bus instead of waiting for callbacks.
how_points: Orchestrator reads the store, not callbacks
After a crash, resume from the store

visual.caption: The loop closes through shared state

days.analogy: A kitchen ticket rail: cooks come and go, but the tickets on the rail say exactly what is done and what is next.

jargon.plain: the database where every unit of work is recorded
a running feed of 'this just happened' messages

days.takeaway: The orchestrator never waits for a callback; it reads shared state, so work survives a crash on either side.
days.artifact: Draw the loop by hand once: orchestrator, sessions, store, back to the orchestrator.
verify: how-gas-city-works.md, 'The machinery underneath': Orchestrator, Bead store, Event bus.
Same page: 'The loop closes through shared state'.

days.title: Why Not a Bash Loop or CI?
days.what: An orchestrator runs work as a graph with a durable memory. A bash loop only restarts an agent; CI only checks a finished change.
days.why: A loop has no model of the work. Every round starts blind, and a crash loses whatever the last round knew.
days.how: The orchestrator holds each step until its dependencies close, fans ready steps out, retries failures and stores every unit durably.

visual.caption: CI is complementary: it verifies the change a formula produces

days.analogy: A loop is an alarm clock that keeps waking you up. An orchestrator is a project manager with a checklist.

jargon.plain: steps joined by 'this finishes before that' arrows
saved, so it survives crashes and restarts

days.takeaway: A loop repeats; an orchestrator remembers.
days.artifact: Write the naive loop on a sticky note as the 'before' picture.
demo: while true; do claude -p "keep working on the task"; done   # the naive loop
verify: FAQ: 'Couldn't I get the same thing from a bash loop or CI?'

days.title: The Toolbelt: gc, bd, tmux, Dolt
days.what: Gas City runs on a small toolbelt: gc drives the city, bd manages beads, tmux hosts sessions and Dolt stores the beads.
days.why: When something breaks, knowing which tool owns which job tells you exactly where to look.
days.how: brew install gascity brings the dependencies, and gc init checks them. Set GC_BEADS=file to skip Dolt and bd while you learn.
how_points: gc init and gc start check prerequisites
Every agent session lives in tmux

visual.caption: One job per tool

days.analogy: A workshop: the foreman's clipboard, the job tickets, the workbenches and the filing cabinet.

jargon.plain: a tool that keeps many terminals running, even in the background
a SQL database with Git-style version history

days.takeaway: Learn which tool owns which job, and every error message gets easier to read.
days.artifact: The prerequisites table from the README: tmux, git, jq, dolt, bd, flock.
demo: export GC_BEADS=file   # skip dolt + bd while learning
verify: README prerequisites table and the GC_BEADS=file note.
FAQ: agent sessions run in tmux.

days.title: City and Rig: The Factory Floor
days.what: A city is the directory holding your agents, formulas and settings. A rig is a project, usually a Git repo, registered with it.
what_points: Each rig gets its own bead prefix
days.why: Work needs a home and a boundary: the city holds the method, and each rig keeps its work apart from other projects.
days.how: gc init creates and starts a city. gc rig add registers a project, gives it a bead prefix and keeps its path in .gc/site.toml.

visual.caption: One city, one rig

days.analogy: The city is the factory building; each rig is a production line for one product.

jargon.plain: a project directory registered with the city
the two letters on every bead ID that show which project it belongs to

days.takeaway: The city is your factory floor; a rig is a project you bring onto it.
days.artifact: Run gc init and gc rig add once, or use the Tutorial 01 transcript on the slide.
verify: Tutorial 01: gc rig add prints 'Prefix: mp'.
Tutorial 01: the rig path binding lives in .gc/site.toml.

days.title: Your First Sling: The Work Lifecycle
days.what: Slinging hands a task to an agent: gc sling creates a bead and routes it, and the city does the rest.
days.why: This is the smallest complete loop. Once you see it, every bigger workflow is more of the same.
days.how: Sling creates a bead and a route. A reconcile tick spawns a session, the agent finds its work, edits the rig and closes the bead.
how_points: Sling creates a bead and a route
The agent works in the rig
The bead closes; events record it

visual.caption: The work lifecycle after one sling

days.analogy: Dropping a ticket in the kitchen window: you don't pick the cook, the kitchen picks it up.

jargon.plain: Gas City's verb for creating work and routing it in one go
the orchestrator's regular check-in, every 30 seconds by default

days.takeaway: One sling sets the whole loop in motion: bead, session, work, close.
days.artifact: The hello-world sling transcript from Tutorial 01.
demo: gc sling my-project/claude "Write hello world in python to the file hello.py"
verify: Tutorial 01: sling prints 'Created mp-…' and attaches the mol-do-work workflow.
health-patrol.md: the patrol interval defaults to 30 seconds.

days.title: The Bead: Work That Survives a Crash
days.what: A bead is one unit of work with an ID, a title, a status and a type.
what_points: Lives in the store, not the agent
days.why: Agents crash and sessions recycle. Because the work lives in a bead, a fresh agent picks up exactly where the last one stopped.
days.how: An agent claims an open bead, which moves it to in progress, and closes it when done. Blocked and deferred are managed for you.
how_points: blocked and deferred: managed for you

visual.caption: A bead's lifecycle

days.analogy: A sticky note on a shared board: whoever picks it up moves it to doing, then done. The note outlives any worker.

jargon.plain: an agent takes a bead in one step, so nobody else works on it

days.takeaway: Sessions are disposable; beads are not.
days.artifact: A bd list output with the status symbols.
verify: Tutorial 06: statuses open, in_progress, blocked, deferred, closed.
Tutorial 06: bead IDs start with a two-letter prefix.

days.title: Everything Is a Bead
days.what: Tasks, mail, sessions and convoys are all beads that differ only by type.
what_points: One store, one way to query
days.why: One store means one way to query, one dependency model and one history. That is what makes the system composable.
days.how: bd list shows formula steps, mail and sessions side by side. A formula run lands as plain task beads tagged with metadata.
how_points: The type column says what it is

visual.caption: Same store, same queries; only the type differs

days.analogy: One spreadsheet with a 'type' column instead of four separate spreadsheets.

jargon.plain: extra key-value notes attached to a bead

days.takeaway: When everything is a bead, one set of tools works on everything.
days.artifact: The bead types table from Tutorial 06.
demo: bd list --status in_progress --flat   # live sessions show up as beads too
verify: Tutorial 06 bead types table: task, message, session, convoy.
Tutorial 06: a formula root carries gc.kind=workflow metadata.

days.title: Dependencies: Order Without a Scheduler
days.what: A dependency says one bead must close before another can start.
days.why: No central scheduler decides what runs next. Agents simply only see work that is ready.
days.how: bd dep A --blocks B adds the edge. B disappears from every agent's work query until A closes; then it shows up as ready.
how_points: B is hidden while A is open

visual.caption: Agents only see ready work

days.analogy: You can't paint a wall before the plaster dries, so the painter isn't even told about the job yet.

jargon.plain: an arrow that links two beads
open, with nothing blocking it

days.takeaway: Agents only see ready work, so the right order emerges from the graph.
days.artifact: Two beads and one blocks edge.
demo: bd ready --unassigned --limit=5   # mc-xp7 stays hidden until mc-a4l closes
verify: Tutorial 06 dependency table: only blocks affects work visibility.
Check the exact bd ready flags on your bd version: bd ready --help.

days.title: Convoys: Track a Batch as One
days.what: A convoy is a bead that groups related beads, so you can track a batch of work as one unit.
what_points: Closes itself when all are done
days.why: Real work comes in batches: a sprint, a deploy, a feature. You want one answer to 'is all of this done yet?'
days.how: gc convoy create links members with tracks edges, which block nothing. When the last member closes, the convoy closes itself.

visual.caption: Convoy membership is tracking, not blocking

days.analogy: A shipping convoy: each truck drives on its own, but you track the convoy's arrival as one event.

jargon.plain: an 'I care about this' link that blocks nothing

days.takeaway: A convoy groups work without making the pieces wait on each other.
days.artifact: The gc convoy status output for 'Sprint 42' from Tutorial 06.
demo: gc convoy create "Sprint 42" mc-ykp mc-a4l mc-xp7
verify: Tutorial 06: convoy membership uses tracks edges.
Tutorial 06: auto-close runs from the on_close hook; owned convoys skip it.

days.title: The Pull Model: How Agents Find Work
days.what: Agents pull their work: each one asks the store for ready work routed to it, then claims one bead.
days.why: Pulling means the sender never needs to know which session exists. Work waits safely until a worker is ready.
days.how: Sling stamps gc.routed_to on the bead. At startup an agent runs gc hook --claim, which claims one ready bead from its queue.

visual.caption: Routing decides which queue; readiness decides when

days.analogy: A taxi rank: passengers queue at the right rank, and the next free taxi takes the next passenger.

jargon.plain: taking a bead in one step, so two agents can never grab the same one

days.takeaway: Routing decides which queue a bead lands in; readiness decides whether anyone can see it.
days.artifact: The generic worker prompt printed by gc prime: claim, show, close, repeat.
demo: gc prime   # the generic worker prompt with gc hook --claim
verify: Tutorial 06, 'How agents find work'.
Tutorial 02: gc prime output.

days.title: Demo: A Tiny Work Graph by Hand
days.what: Today we build a three-bead work graph by hand with bd and watch readiness change as beads close.
days.why: Doing it by hand once makes the factory's automatic behaviour obvious. A formula creates exactly this, only bigger.
days.how: Create three beads, add a blocks edge, group them in a convoy, close the blocker and watch the convoy's progress.
how_points: bd close A, then B is ready

lines: $ gc convoy create "Landing page" mc-1 mc-2 mc-3
$ bd close mc-1                    # mc-2 is now ready
visual.caption: Week two in seven commands

days.analogy: Laying out the ingredients and recipe steps by hand before letting the kitchen run them.
days.takeaway: A formula simply creates this graph for you, and now you know exactly what it builds.
days.artifact: Run the seven commands in a scratch city (GC_BEADS=file is fine) and keep the convoy status output.
verify: Real bead IDs differ from mc-1, mc-2, mc-3: use the IDs bd prints.
Tutorial 06: gc convoy create syntax.

days.title: Agents: A Role Is a Prompt
days.what: An agent is a configured worker: a name, a provider, a scope and a prompt template that defines its behaviour.
days.why: Because a role is just a prompt you wrote, a new reviewer, planner or tester takes minutes. No plugin, no code.
why_points: As many roles as you need
days.how: gc agent add scaffolds the folder. agent.toml sets provider and scope; the prompt says how to work. gc prime shows the result.

lines: Review the code: bugs, security, style.
visual.caption: A reviewer is two small files

days.analogy: A job description: the same person becomes a reviewer or a planner depending on the description you hand over.

jargon.plain: the coding-agent CLI that runs the agent, such as Claude Code or Codex
the starting instructions, filled in with details about the city

days.takeaway: A reviewer is nothing more than the prompt you wrote for it.
days.artifact: The reviewer agent folder from Tutorial 02.
verify: Tutorial 02: agent.toml with dir and provider.
how-gas-city-works.md: the prompt template is the agent's entire behavioural spec.

days.title: Harnesses: One Fleet, Many Coding Agents
days.what: Each agent picks its own harness, such as Claude Code, Codex or Gemini CLI, so a mixed fleet is just configuration.
days.why: Different models are good at different jobs. Mixing them puts the right model on the right role without changing the workflow.
days.how: Set provider in agent.toml and register it in city.toml. An agent has five axes: harness, model, upstream, transport, runtime.

visual.caption: Five axes you can tune per agent

days.analogy: A band where each musician brings their own instrument, but everyone reads the same sheet music.

jargon.plain: the coding-agent program an agent runs inside
the service that actually serves the model

days.takeaway: In Gas City, a mixed fleet of coding agents is just configuration.
days.artifact: Two agent.toml snippets side by side: one Claude, one Codex.
demo: gc doctor --fix   # adds missing builtin provider aliases
verify: FAQ: sixteen built-in harnesses.
configuring-an-agent.md: the five axes.
Tutorial 02: register [providers.codex] with base = "builtin:codex".

days.title: Sessions: On-Demand vs. Always-On
days.what: A session is a running agent: a live process with its own terminal, state and conversation history.
days.why: On-demand sessions save cost: they start for work and stop when idle. Always-on sessions keep a coordinator ready to chat.
days.how: Slung work starts on-demand sessions. A named session with mode always stays alive. Watch with peek and logs; poke with nudge.

visual.caption: Same primitive, two lifecycles

days.analogy: Contractors who come in for a job, versus a receptionist who's always at the front desk.

jargon.plain: a session with a stable name the city keeps track of
typing a message straight into a running session

days.takeaway: Agents are definitions; sessions are the live processes, and they're disposable by design.
days.artifact: gc session list output with a reviewer that is creating and a mayor that is active.
verify: Tutorial 03: the on-demand vs. always-on table.
Tutorial 03: detach from tmux with Ctrl-b d.

days.title: Agents Talk Only Through the Store
days.what: Agents never call each other. They coordinate through the bead store: mail for messages, sling for delegated work.
days.why: With no references between agents, any of them can crash, restart, scale or switch providers without breaking the others.
days.how: A human mails the mayor. The mayor plans and slings tasks to agents, and agents close their beads. Every hop goes through the store.
how_points: A nudge only wakes a live session

visual.caption: Agents coordinate only through the store

days.analogy: A shared office mailroom: nobody walks into anyone's office; everything goes through the pigeonholes.

jargon.plain: a persistent message stored as a bead
a one-off poke into a live terminal that isn't saved

days.takeaway: No agent holds a reference to another, so any of them can crash, scale or swap.
days.artifact: The mail vs. nudge table from Tutorial 04.
demo: gc mail send mayor -s "Review needed" -m "Please look at the auth changes"
verify: Tutorial 04 table: mail survives a crash, a nudge does not.

days.title: Hooks: Wiring a Coding Agent Into the City
days.what: Hooks connect a plain coding-agent process to Gas City, so it receives mail, picks up work and saves a hand-off by itself.
what_points: gc init wires Claude for you
days.why: Without hooks you'd run gc mail check and gc prime by hand, on every agent, every turn.
days.how: gc init writes a managed .gc/settings.json for Claude. It runs Gas City commands at session start, before each turn and before compaction.
how_points: Each turn: deliver mail and nudges

visual.caption: Three moments where Gas City steps in

days.analogy: Phone notifications: apps don't keep asking you; the phone taps them on the shoulder at the right moment.

jargon.plain: when a coding agent summarises its conversation to free up memory

days.takeaway: Hooks turn a bare coding agent into a member of the city.
days.artifact: The install_agent_hooks line for a non-Claude provider.
verify: Tutorial 04: Claude is the only provider wired automatically.
Tutorial 04: hooks fire at session start, before each turn and before compaction.

days.title: Pools: Scaling Workers to Demand
days.what: A pool is one agent definition scaled into several identical workers that share a single queue.
days.why: Ten ready tasks shouldn't wait on one worker, and zero tasks shouldn't keep ten sessions running.
days.how: Each tick the orchestrator runs the agent's scale_check to measure demand, then sizes the pool between its floor and cap.

visual.caption: Demand in, sessions out

days.analogy: Supermarket checkouts: open more lanes when the queue grows, close them when it's quiet.

jargon.plain: a small command that reports how much new work is waiting
Gas Town names for persistent and transient workers: operating styles, not types

days.takeaway: A pool turns one agent definition into exactly as many workers as the work needs.
days.artifact: The pool line from gc status in Tutorial 01: 'scaled (min=0, max=2)'.
demo: gc status   # look for a line like: scaled (min=0, max=2)
verify: docs/reference/config.md: scale_check, min_active_sessions, max_active_sessions.
coming-from-gastown.md: crew and polecats are operating modes, not types.

days.title: Demo: Build a Reviewer and Sling a Review
days.what: Today we define a reviewer agent, sling it a review and watch its session do the work.
days.why: This recap ties week three together: role, harness, session, pull model and coordination, in one small run.
days.how: Scaffold the agent, write its prompt, sling a review, peek at the session and read the result.
how_points: gc session peek, then read review.md

lines: $ gc sling my-project/reviewer "Review hello.py and write review.md"
visual.caption: Week three in one run

days.analogy: Hiring a specialist, handing them a ticket and glancing through the window while they work.
days.takeaway: A role, a prompt and one sling: that's a new specialist on your factory floor.
days.artifact: Record the terminal run beforehand, or show the transcript on the slide.
demo: gc sling my-project/reviewer "Review hello.py and write review.md with feedback"
verify: Tutorial 02: a custom agent has no default sling formula, so the bead is delivered directly.
Tutorial 02: the 'suggest' permission mode blocks unattended writes; use a non-blocking mode for slung work.

days.title: Formulas: Write the Method Down Once
days.what: A formula is a TOML file that records how a job gets done: its steps, their dependencies and its variables.
days.why: A method kept in a prompt is improvised every time. Written down, it's repeatable, reviewable and runs across many agents.
days.how: Steps declare needs. Steps without needs run in parallel. Pancakes: dry and wet together, then combine, cook and serve.

visual.caption: The pancakes formula as a graph

days.analogy: A recipe card: anyone can cook from it, and two people can mix dry and wet ingredients at the same time.

jargon.plain: a simple, readable config file format
a graph of steps with arrows and no loops

days.takeaway: Write the method down once, and the orchestrator can run it again and again.
days.artifact: formulas/pancakes.toml from Tutorial 05.
verify: Tutorial 05: a formula isn't the work itself (that's a bead); it's the reusable method.
Tutorial 05: the v2 compiler rejects cycles at compile time.

days.title: From TOML to Beads: Cook vs. Sling
days.what: Applying a formula compiles it into a recipe, then turns every step into a bead in the store.
days.why: Once the steps are beads, the run no longer depends on the file or on any session. A crash can't erase it.
days.how: gc formula cook creates the beads without routing. gc sling with --formula creates and routes. A finalize step is added.

visual.caption: File, recipe, beads

days.analogy: Printing tickets from a recipe: the recipe stays in the book, and the printed tickets go on the rail.

jargon.plain: turn a plan into real records in the store
a step the orchestrator completes itself; no agent works on it

days.takeaway: A formula is the method; applying it prints the work as beads that outlive everything.
days.artifact: The gc formula cook pancakes output: a root and 'Created: 7'.
verify: Tutorial 05: 'Created: 7' is the root, five steps and the finalize step.
Tutorial 05: sling doesn't prompt the agent by default; --nudge does.

days.title: Variables: One Method, Many Runs
days.what: Variables make a formula reusable: declare them, use {{name}} in the steps and pass values when you cook or sling.
days.why: The same review or release method should work for any branch, feature or priority, without copying the file.
days.how: Variables stay placeholders through compilation and are filled in only when beads are created. Fields validate the input.

visual.caption: gc formula cook feature-work --var title="Auth overhaul"

days.analogy: A form letter: the same letter with a different name and date each time.

jargon.plain: values are filled in at the last moment, when the work is created

days.takeaway: Variables turn one written method into a method for every situation.
days.artifact: The feature-work formula with title, branch and priority.
demo: gc formula show feature-work --var title="Auth system"
verify: Tutorial 05 variable fields: description, required, default, enum, pattern.
Tutorial 05: a variable without a default that isn't required stays as the literal {{name}}.

days.title: v1 vs. v2 Formulas: Who Is the Engine?
days.what: Formulas have two contracts. In v1 the agent you sling to is the engine; in v2 the orchestrator is the engine.
what_points: v1: one agent runs it all
v2: the orchestrator runs a graph
days.why: Only v2 makes each step its own routable bead, so steps can go to different agents, run in parallel and retry on their own.
days.how: Opt in with a [requires] table. v1 builds a parent-child molecule; v2 builds a flat graph of blocking edges with a finalize step.
how_points: v2: a flat graph plus finalize

visual.caption: Two contracts, two engines

days.analogy: v1 is one chef cooking the whole menu. v2 is a head chef sending each dish to the right station.

jargon.plain: v1's container bead with its steps as children
the set of rules a formula is compiled under

days.takeaway: In v2 the orchestrator, not a single agent, is the engine.
days.artifact: The v1 vs. v2 comparison table from Understanding Formulas.
verify: understanding-formulas.md contract table: engine, steps, control flow, routing, shape.
understanding-formulas.md: 'For new work, choose v2.'

days.title: Check and Retry: Work That Verifies Itself
days.what: check reruns a step until a script says it passed. retry re-dispatches a step that failed for a temporary reason.
what_points: Both run while the workflow runs
days.why: An agent saying 'done' isn't proof. A check makes done mean verified, and retry absorbs flaky failures without a human.
days.how: A check script runs after each attempt: exit 0 means done, anything else starts another attempt, up to max_attempts.

visual.loop_label: non-zero exit: next attempt, up to max_attempts
visual.caption: The step is done when the script says so

days.analogy: A driving test: you're licensed when the examiner signs off, not when you say you can drive.

jargon.plain: the number a script returns; 0 means success

days.takeaway: With check, done means verified, not just claimed.
days.artifact: The 'checked' formula with scripts/verify.sh from Tutorial 05.
verify: Tutorial 05: check is v2-only.
Tutorial 05: exit code 75 re-runs the check without spending an attempt.
understanding-formulas.md: check and retry are mutually exclusive on the same step.

days.title: Drain: Fan Out Over a Convoy
days.what: drain runs one small workflow per member of a convoy, all in parallel, for a set of work found only at runtime.
what_points: The set is known only at runtime
days.why: You rarely know in advance how many tasks a plan will produce. Drain scales the fan-out to whatever is in the convoy now.
days.how: A drain step names an item formula. The orchestrator splits the convoy into one-member units and runs the item formula for each.

visual.caption: drain fans a convoy out into parallel runs

days.analogy: A teacher handing each student one worksheet from the pile, however many students showed up today.

jargon.plain: splitting one job into many parallel jobs
a separate checkout of the same Git repo, for parallel work

days.takeaway: Drain turns a convoy of any size into parallel, isolated runs.
days.artifact: The build-from-convoy drain step from Understanding Formulas.
verify: understanding-formulas.md: drain is the canonical v2 fan-out.

days.title: Demo: Write and Run the Pancakes Formula
days.what: Today we write the pancakes formula, preview it, cook it into beads and sling it to an agent.
days.why: This recap connects week four: method, compilation, beads and the orchestrator driving the graph to done.
days.how: Write formulas/pancakes.toml, preview it with gc formula show, then cook it, sling the root and watch the beads close.

visual.caption: gc formula show pancakes lists 6 steps, including finalize

days.analogy: Cooking from the recipe card you wrote last week, with two helpers mixing in parallel.
days.takeaway: Write the method, preview it, run it, and the orchestrator drives it to done.
days.artifact: A working pancakes.toml in your scratch city.
verify: Tutorial 05: gc formula show prints 6 steps, including workflow-finalize.

days.title: Orders: When, Not How
days.what: An order pairs a trigger with an action, so a formula or script runs on a schedule, a condition or an event.
days.why: Formulas say how; orders say when. Together, the factory starts its own work: nightly checks, updates, release notes.
why_points: Drop in a file, no restart
days.how: Put a TOML file in orders/. Triggers: cooldown, cron, condition, event, manual. Cooldown drifts; cron hits fixed clock times.

visual.caption: Cooldown drifts; cron keeps clock time

days.analogy: A thermostat: you set the rule once, and it turns the heating on by itself.

jargon.plain: wait a fixed interval after the last run
run at fixed clock times, such as 3 a.m. every day

days.takeaway: Formulas say how; orders say when, and then nobody has to press go.
days.artifact: orders/pancakes-check.toml: cooldown, 5m, pool worker.
verify: Tutorial 07: the orchestrator ticks every 30 seconds.
Tutorial 07: trigger types table.

days.title: Exec Orders: Automation Without an LLM
days.what: An exec order runs a shell script on the orchestrator: no agent, no model, no work beads.
days.why: Pruning branches or checking disk space needs no intelligence. A script is cheaper, faster and more predictable.
days.how: Set exec to a script instead of formula. Exec orders take no pool, get ORDER_DIR in their environment and time out after 300 seconds.

visual.caption: Every order has a formula or an exec, never both

days.analogy: You don't hire a consultant to take out the bins; you set a reminder.

jargon.plain: run a program directly

days.takeaway: Use agents for judgment and scripts for chores.
days.artifact: The prune-merged exec order snippet from Tutorial 07.
demo: gc order list   # built-in housekeeping orders such as reaper and gate-sweep
verify: Tutorial 07: exec orders can't have a pool.
Tutorial 07: default timeouts are 30 s for formula orders and 300 s for exec orders.

days.title: Health Patrol: Let It Crash
days.what: Health patrol is the orchestrator's supervision loop: it keeps running sessions in line with your config and restarts failures.
days.why: Agents will crash. Rather than prevent every crash, Gas City makes crashes cheap: the work persists and a fresh session resumes it.
days.how: Each tick compares what config wants with what runs: start missing agents, stop orphans, restart drifted ones.

visual.caption: Reconciliation, the Erlang/OTP way

days.analogy: A lifeguard doesn't stop people swimming; they watch and pull out anyone in trouble.

jargon.plain: make what's running match what the config says
stop restarting an agent that keeps crashing, for a while

days.takeaway: Gas City doesn't prevent crashes; it makes them cheap.
days.artifact: The three reconciliation rules: start missing, stop orphans, restart drifted.
demo: gc session reset mayor   # bead, mail and queued work survive
verify: health-patrol.md: Erlang/OTP supervision and 'let it crash'.
health-patrol.md: crash loop quarantine is in memory only.

days.title: Events: Watching the Fleet
days.what: An event is an unchangeable record fired when something happens: a bead closes, a session crashes, an order fires.
days.why: You can't steer a fleet you can't see. Events let you and other agents watch everything, and even trigger new work.
days.how: Each event has a sequence number, so watchers resume where they stopped. Event-triggered orders read the same stream.

visual.caption: You, agents and orders all read the same stream

days.analogy: A departures board: nobody calls you; the board updates and you react.

jargon.plain: an always-increasing counter, so you can resume where you stopped

days.takeaway: Events let humans watch the factory, and let the factory react to itself.
days.artifact: A short gc events --follow capture, or the dashboard.
verify: how-gas-city-works.md: event names such as bead.created, session.crashed, order.fired.
dashboard.md: gc dashboard opens the supervisor's dashboard.

days.title: Packs: What Configures the Factory
days.what: A pack is a directory with a pack.toml that declares agents, formulas and orders. Your city is itself a pack.
days.why: Coordination that lives in chat and in people's heads leaks. A pack turns it into versioned files you can review and share.
days.how: Everything sorts into three layers: the portable pack, deployment choices in city.toml, and machine-local state in .gc/.
how_points: Start small; move what you repeat

visual.caption: From hand-rolled to a city: three layers

days.analogy: A franchise manual: recipes and job roles are the same in every branch, and each branch picks its own address.

jargon.plain: machine-specific settings, such as where a repo lives on this laptop

days.takeaway: A pack turns how your team works into versioned, shareable files.
days.artifact: The three-layer table from the multi-agent engineering environment guide.
verify: multi-agent-engineering-environment.md: the three layers table.
understanding-packs.md: a pack with an unknown schema is rejected whole.

days.title: Imports: Reuse Without Copying
days.what: An import pulls a shared pack into your city, so its agents, formulas and orders work as if you'd written them.
days.why: Teams shouldn't fork a pack to change one setting. Imports plus patches reuse a pack and override only what differs.
days.how: The binding qualifies names: [imports.review] gives review.reviewer, or checkout-service/review.reviewer for a rig import.

visual.caption: The binding qualifies the name; the rig adds a prefix

days.analogy: Adding a library to a project: you use it by name and pin the version you trust.

jargon.plain: the local name you give an imported pack
a small change applied to something that already exists

days.takeaway: Import packs, pin versions, patch the differences, and never fork.
days.artifact: The [imports.gc] block from the pack.toml in Tutorial 01.
verify: understanding-packs.md: city imports give gc.planner; rig imports give checkout-service/gc.planner.
understanding-packs.md: a patch changes an existing agent; it never creates one.

days.title: The Whole Job, End to End
days.what: A real build is a pipeline of everything we've learned: decompose, drain, review, gap-check, fix, check and ship.
days.why: This is Day 1's promise: describe a feature once and come back to a finished branch, at production quality and machine speed.
days.how: The formula is the method, the beads are the work and the orchestrator is the engine, all outside any agent's session.

visual.caption: One body of work, end to end

days.analogy: Day 1's restaurant, fully open: recipes, stations, tickets, a head chef and a pass where every plate is checked.

jargon.plain: comparing the result with the plan to find what's missing

days.takeaway: Write the method once, and the factory turns it into finished work.
